title: The power of the weekly review
author: Anne-Laure Le Cunff
summary: Le Cunff makes the case for a fixed weekly self-review as the corrective to working through a task list without ever asking whether the tasks serve a goal. Her argument is that a daily to-do list measures motion rather than direction, and that an hour of structured reflection each week is the cheapest available safeguard against productivity for its own sake. She distinguishes the practice from journaling: journaling confronts thoughts and feelings, while the weekly review looks back at what worked and forward at what to plan. The practical core is the Plus Minus Next template, three columns for what went well, what did not, and what comes next, optionally supplemented by growth mindset prompts about struggles, learning goals and who to ask for help. The second half is about turning the review into a ritual, with advice to fix the day, time and place, to stay compassionate after bad weeks, and to keep revising the template itself. Le Cunff frames the review as deliberate metacognition rather than another productivity chore.
points: The weekly review is positioned as a decision-making tool rather than a productivity tool, aimed at checking whether tasks still point at the goals.
Plus Minus Next gives the practice a three column structure that is fast enough to survive contact with a busy week.
Growth mindset prompts extend the review outward, asking what to learn, what to try outside the comfort zone, and who to approach for help.
Le Cunff insists on a consistent day, time and place so the ritual does not consume cognitive load in scheduling itself.
She treats the template as provisional, arguing that evaluating your own review process is part of the review.
quotes: Every Sunday evening, I sit down for a weekly review. It’s easy to mindlessly go through a task list without ever stopping to ask whether these tasks align with our goals.

Checking tasks off a daily to-do list is not enough to make meaningful progress in life and work. While a weekly review may seem like additional work, it’s a great safeguard against productivity for the sake of productivity.
While journaling is mostly about confronting your thoughts and emotions, the weekly review is about reflecting on what went well and what didn’t during the past week, and planning for the week ahead.

There are many weekly review templates out there. Some are longer, others are shorter; some have a fixed framework to follow, others are more flexible. What ultimately matters is to find an approach you can actually stick to, so it becomes part of your weekly routine.

Pick a consistent day, time, and place. Consistency is key in building habits. Don’t add to your cognitive load by repeatedly asking yourself when and where you should sit down to write your weekly review.
Be kind to yourself. Don’t beat yourself up when you had a bad week and didn’t achieve the goals you set up for yourself. A weekly review is as much retrospective as it is prospective.

You will notice that a week rarely turns out how you imagined it. And that’s alright. The weekly review is an opportunity to practice metacognition and become more aware of your productivity and thought processes.
